summary:
Visa requirements for the Netherlands depend on nationality alone. Transgender and non-binary visitors are not treated differently in visa applications, and a passport carrying a gender marker other than the one assigned at birth, or an 'X' marker, is accepted for entry provided it was officially issued. No additional gender documentation may be demanded at the border.

Discrimination on grounds of gender identity is prohibited. Gender expression became an explicitly protected ground under the Equal Treatment Act in March 2019, following passage by the House of Representatives in 2018 (127 votes to 23) and the Senate on 12 March 2019 (64 to 11), after the Netherlands Institute for Human Rights had already treated transgender people as covered by the word 'gender' in earlier cases. Since February 2023, sexual orientation and disability are formally written into Article 1 of the Constitution.

Since 1 July 2025, a discriminatory motive is codified in Dutch law as a ground for increasing penalties in criminal cases, operating alongside expanded victims' rights and protection of victim data. Dutch legislation nonetheless contains no statutory definition of 'hate crime'; police record hate crimes, hate speech and other discrimination incidents through the police Centre of Expertise Discrimination (ECAD-P), which is the framework behind published hate-crime statistics.

Reported anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination is rising. Police recorded 4,800 discrimination and violence reports about LGBTQIA+ people last year, up 7.5% on 2024 and up 81% from 2,654 in 2022, with reports concerning transgender people up 51% in a year (264 to 399). The COC described the figures as extremely worrying and noted only six convictions for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination in the same year. Official Dutch government figures state that over 10% of LGBTIQ+ people have experienced physical or sexual violence, including 17% of transgender people and 22% of intersex people, and that incidents of verbal abuse, intimidation and violence rose sharply per the 2023 National Programme against Discrimination and Racism; in 2022, one third of police discrimination reports concerned sexual orientation.

During WorldPride Amsterdam 2026, more than 70 people reported discrimination through the RITA platform in the opening period, mostly festival-goers leaving the Milkshake festival and Pride Walk participants; RITA warned the reports are only a fraction of the total. Amsterdam broadened 'Safer Spaces' reporting points for anti-LGBTQIA+ violence during World Pride to cover the Nieuwe Kerk, the Stedelijk Museum, the Stadsarchief, hotels and a central RITA location, with 1.4 million visitors expected. Mayor Femke Halsema told the council that Amsterdam will tackle discrimination and violent incidents with priority during World Pride, with police, enforcer and organiser agreements to act fast; recent Prides drew 25 to 45 anti-LGBTQIA+ incident reports covering vandalism, theft, discrimination, insults, intimidation and serious assault, typically with perpetrators fleeing the scene.

Legal gender change in the Netherlands still requires a medical expert letter, falling short of self-determination. The 'X' marker is available only through a court procedure taking three to nine months, and the Transgender Act (self-ID) was withdrawn in July 2025. Compensation was offered to people sterilised under earlier rules. Legal gender recognition has otherwise been administrative since a December 2013 law took effect in 2014, removing the earlier requirement of surgery and sterilisation imposed by the 1984-85 laws.

Transgender detainees occupy an unregulated space in Dutch law. No law, regulation or official policy governs their placement: the Penitentiary Principles Act only separates male and female detainees, and the Prison Service (DJI) confirmed placement is based on the gender designation in the municipal records (BRP) together with case-by-case factors such as gender-related physical features, the detainee's own preference, offence background, and physical or mental health. The Netherlands Jurists Committee for Human Rights (NJCM) advised the caretaker Minister for Legal Protection, Robine van der Meer and later Minister Weerwind, in a letter of 21 February 2024 that this absence of rules is worrying and undesirable, noting international research documenting human-rights violations including discrimination and sexual violence against transgender detainees, the absence of official figures on the number of transgender detainees, and the relevance of CPT standards. Transgender detainees are frequently placed on an 'Extra Care Facility' (EZV) wing, generally to protect them from other detainees, where they sit alongside people with intellectual disabilities and sex offenders. Documented cases include a trans woman initially held on a regular male wing before transfer to an EZV; a parole-board appeals ruling of 21 March 2016 (15/4323/GB) concerning a trans woman first placed in a men's institution before transfer to the women's prison at Nieuwersluis, who reported intimidation, threats, assaults and molestation; and rulings by the Limburg court (17 October 2017, ECLI:NL:RBLIM:2017:10624) and The Hague appeals court (29 June 2020, ECLI:NL:GHDHA:2020:1108) treating a wing not matching the detainee's gender as making imprisonment considerably heavier. NJCM asked the minister to create CPT-aligned rules placing transgender detainees by gender identity; the DIZ said it was drafting guidelines, unpublished at the time.

Access to care: Dutch insurance fully covers PrPreP and related care for gay and bisexual men from 1 August 2019 at all Municipal Health Services (GGD) offices. Assisted insemination for infertility is covered by health insurance regardless of whether the patient is single, in an opposite-sex couple or a lesbian couple. The 2016 Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport guidelines, endorsed by eight medical organisations including the Dutch Psychiatry Association and Transvisie, recommend puberty blockers for transgender adolescents at Tanner Stage II with informed consent and endocrinologist approval, and top surgery is available to patients over 16. In July 2026 the Dutch Health Board reaffirmed gender-affirming care for trans youth, citing harms of delay, mental-health improvements and a low regret rate. Conversion therapy has been excluded from health insurance coverage since June 2012 and the practice was banned by a bill ratified on 8 September 2026.

Open military service has been permitted for gay people since homosexuality's declassification as a mental illness in 1973 and for transgender people as well. Equaldex records the Netherlands as recognising non-binary gender, protecting bathroom access, and prohibiting discrimination in employment and housing on sexual orientation and gender identity grounds, while noting that hate-crime protections cover sexual orientation only. The Netherlands ranks 13th on the ILGA Rainbow Map 2026.
tangentialFactors:
Public attitudes are shifting. The Utrecht University/Trimbos HBSC study found positive attitudes toward homosexuality among secondary-school boys dropped from 40% to 22% and among girls from 78% to 51% between 2021 and 2025, a decline in acceptance among adolescents over the period. A 2018 Statistics Netherlands survey found 11.4% of LGBTQ youth faced online bullying and harassment, more than double the rate for heterosexual young people, and a 2020 Movisie estimate put homeless LGBTQ youth at 900 to 2,000, three times the rate for heterosexual youth, with rejection at home a stated cause.

Equaldex records high public support, with 22% support for LGBT openness in one measure and a ranking of 2nd of 121 regions as a 'good place' for LGBT people; these aggregate figures sit alongside the rising incident reports recorded by police.

The Netherlands' legal framework compares favourably with regional peers on formal protections: homosexuality is legal, marriage is legal, gender change is legal though requiring a medical diagnosis, discrimination is illegal, and conversion therapy is banned. The gap between formal protection and enforcement is visible in the low conviction count for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination relative to report volume.

outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the withdrawn Transgender Act has been replaced by any successor legislation after July 2025 is not sourced in the inventory; the current status rests on the Outright International update of March 2026.
